b: Fall is one of the most exciting times of the year to target brown trout and steelhead as they make their pilgrimage into tributaries and feeder rivers or creeks. With water temperatures beginning to drop and fish preparing for the colder months ahead, their feeding habits and locations can change dramatically.

Whether fishing Great Lakes tributaries, smaller streams, or larger rivers, understanding what trout are eating can be the difference between a slow day and a memorable one. Matching the hatch is often associated with fly fishing, but it is just as important for anglers throwing conventional tackle. Identifying what food sources are available and choosing presentations that imitate them is one of the best ways to consistently catch trout through the fall. Here’s what you need to know.

One of the first things I pay attention to when approaching a river in the fall is what’s happening around me. Insects, baitfish, and salmon eggs all play important roles in the diets of trout during this time of year.

For brown trout, fall is particularly important because it coincides with their spawning season. As browns move toward spawning areas, they become increasingly focused on reproduction — but that doesn’t mean they stop feeding. In fact, larger browns can be aggressive toward anything that looks like an easy meal. Minnows, sculpins, crayfish, and aquatic insects can all be important food sources.

Steelhead have a slightly different approach. While they primarily enter tributaries to feed and eventually spawn, they remain opportunistic feeders. Insects, small baitfish, and drifting eggs can all trigger strikes. In Great Lakes tributaries, eggs become an especially important food source as salmon and brown trout begin spawning.
Recognizing the present food sources should be your starting point for selecting a bait or fly. If you’re not matching what they’re eating, they won’t bite well.

If there is one food source that becomes especially important in Great Lakes tributaries during the fall, it’s eggs. With salmon, brown trout, and other species spawning throughout the season, rivers can become full of drifting eggs.

For steelhead, a single egg drifting naturally through a feeding lane can be an easy meal. That’s why egg patterns are some of the most productive flies for fall steelhead. Single egg flies, beads, and small egg clusters are all popular options.

Color can make a big difference. Orange, peach, pink, chartreuse, and more natural-looking egg colors all have their place. Freshly deposited eggs may look different from eggs that have been drifting downstream for some time, so experimenting with colors can help determine what fish prefer.

When fishing beads or egg flies, presentation is just as important as color. A natural drift through the strike zone is critical. Fish often have plenty of opportunities to inspect drifting eggs, especially in heavily pressured tributaries, like the Salmon or Niagara River here in New York. Keeping your presentation close to the current’s natural speed can help convince even wary fish.

Eggs are important, but don’t forget about baitfish when targeting larger fall trout. Fall is a great time to encounter some of the year’s biggest browns and steelhead, and these fish are more than willing to eat a substantial meal. Minnows, juvenile baitfish, and sculpins are all potential targets for hungry browns. This is where streamers really shine for fly fishermen. Woolly Buggers, sculpin patterns, and baitfish streamers can all produce aggressive strikes.

Conventional anglers can have similar success with small swimbaits, minnow-style jerkbaits, inline spinners, and other moving baits. Natural baitfish colors such as silver, white, olive, and black are all excellent choices. Some of my favorites include a Keitech Easy Shiner, Rapala Husky Jerk, and a Blue Fox Vibrax. (You can check out our Best Trout Lures buyer’s guide for more of our favorite trout lures, too.)

I particularly like using a baitfish imitation around deeper pools, undercut banks, current seams, and other areas where larger fish can ambush prey. A slow, deliberate retrieve can be extremely effective, especially when water temperatures begin dropping. Don’t be afraid to experiment with larger presentations. Matching the hatch doesn’t always mean fishing small. If the available forage consists of larger minnows, your presentation should reflect that.
Adjusting to Water Conditions and Fishing Pressure

Matching the hatch isn’t just about identifying what trout are eating. It also means adjusting your presentation to the conditions in front of you. After a heavy rain, tributaries may become stained and carry additional food downstream. Fish can become more aggressive, and brighter or larger presentations may help them locate your offering. During low, clear water conditions, however, trout can become extremely cautious. This is when smaller presentations, natural colors, and lighter leaders come into play. Watching the weather can be crucial during the fall, as it can trigger some incredible bite windows.

Fishing pressure is another factor you should consider. Popular fall tributaries can receive plenty of attention from anglers, so fish quickly become familiar with common presentations. If everyone is throwing bright beads, switching to a more natural egg color or an entirely different food imitation might be the ticket. Being different even in the slightest way can make or break your day of fishing.
Pay attention to how fish react. If you’re getting follows but no commitments, try changing the size, color, or retrieve before abandoning an area.
Let the Fish Tell You What They Want

One of the biggest mistakes anglers make is sticking with the same presentation throughout the day. Trout constantly respond to changing conditions, and their feeding preferences can change with them. Start by observing the river. Look for insect activity, spawning fish, baitfish, and areas of natural food collection. From there, choose a presentation that makes sense for the conditions.

Fall brown trout and steelhead fishing offers some incredible opportunities, particularly in Great Lakes tributaries. Whether you’re drifting egg patterns, swinging streamers, fishing beads, or throwing small artificial baits, understanding the available food sources will help you make better decisions.

At the end of the day, matching the hatch is about more than choosing the right color fly or lure. It’s about understanding the environment, recognizing what trout are feeding on, and presenting something that looks natural. Put those puzzle pieces together, and you’ll be much more prepared to take advantage of everything fall trout fishing has to offer.
